newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-CAVEGN BOOSTS SWISS MORALE WITH FAST TIME.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-CAVEGN BOOSTS SWISS MORALE WITH FAST TIME.

text.p: Franco Cavegn lifted the morale of the Swiss men's downhill team at the Alpine skiing world championships by posting the fastest time in Wednesday's second training session.
"I was not aiming to be the fastest today but my good time has helped bring our team out of a black hole," said Cavegn. "This is just what we needed."
The Swiss suffered a blow in Tuesday's first of three training runs when their best-placed skier was 1993 downhill world champion Urs Lehmann in 17th.

The ski-crazed Alpine nation has not won a gold medal in the men's events at world championships since Lehmann, while their last women's title dates back to 1991 when Vreni Schneider took the slalom and Chantal Bournissen the combined.
The Swiss men have not won a World Cup downhill this season and only William Besse made the podium when he was second in Bormio and third in the two-run sprint race in Kitzbuehel.
On Wednesday, Swiss coaches were relieved when their best three downhillers landed in the top nine.
Cavegn clocked one minute 39.45 on a shortened version of the Kandahar Banchetta piste -- which will serve as Thursday's combination slope.
Organisers were forced to lower the starting hut because of heavy winds and poor visibility in the upper part of the course.
Markus Herrmann, who is still fighting with Lehmann for the fourth Swiss starting bib, was seventh best in 1:40.31, while Bruno Kernen was ninth with 1:40.34.
Lehmann and Besse disappointed with only the 24th and 18th fastest times respectively.
The Swiss had been due to announce their final team on Wednesday but pushed the decision back to after Friday's final training run because of the weather.
Despite his good performance, Cavegn was not excited about the piste and said: "At world championships the downhill should be difficult and made for champions and not for everyone."
Frenchman Luc Alphand, currently on antibiotics to cure a bout of influenza, was again second-best, in 1:39.45, and again complained about the lack of difficulty on the piste.
"I would enjoy my runs a lot more if the piste was faster," said Alphand, the 1996 world championship downhill bronze medallist and current leader of the discipline's World Cup.
Local hero Kristian Ghedina, last year's downhill silver medallist, was joint seventh with Herrmann. "I took it easy today," he said.
Austria's defending downhill champion Patrick Ortlieb was sixth quickest and said: "It was very windy and foggy up there."
Ortlieb, the 1994 Olympic downhill champion, said the final jump before the finish area was dangerous because the strong wind lifted a skier up too high in the air.
Norwegian Audun Groenvold crashed on the jump but the former ski jumper walked away without serious injury.
